turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hi. Um, thank you for seeing me. It’s... gosh, where do I start? I guess the main reason I'm actually sitting in this chair right now is because of my job. I do general maintenance and repair—mostly commercial buildings, you know, fixing whatever breaks, HVAC, plumbing, drywall, you name it. I’ve been doing it a really long time and I know my stuff, but... I just keep forgetting things. 

And not just little things, like where I put my coffee. I keep forgetting scheduled callbacks. Like, a tenant will ask me when a replacement part is coming in, and I’ll look them right in the eye and say, "I'll call you first thing Thursday," and I mean it, I really do! But Thursday comes and goes and it doesn't even cross my mind until they're calling the front office angry. And it’s work orders, too. I’ll get a ticket, and I'll be on my way to do it, and then someone stops me in the hallway to ask a quick question about a leaky faucet, and suddenly that original work order is just completely wiped from my brain. 

Even just basic follow-ups I promised people, like telling my boss I finished prepping a unit... I just blank on it. It’s piled up so much lately. The missed tickets, the angry phone calls from people waiting on me. It got so bad that my supervisor actually pulled me aside last week. We had this whole long sit-down in his office, and honestly, work is the one who sent me here. They basically told me I needed to come see someone because there’s a lead maintenance position opening up soon. I really want it, and I’ve put in the years, but they told me flat out that I need to get this sorted out right now before I completely lose my shot at moving up. So... yeah. I just can't keep dropping the ball, but I don't know how to stop doing it.

symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient describes failing to finish workplace duties, such as missing tickets and not completing work orders they were on their way to do.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as someone stopping them in the hallway, which causes them to completely forget their original task.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient explicitly states they keep forgetting daily work activities, such as scheduled callbacks, work orders, and basic follow-ups.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back, did you struggle with staying organized, focused, or remembering things when you were growing up in school?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, gosh, yes. It’s funny you ask that because, you know, sometimes I try to tell myself, "Oh, it’s just the stress of the building, it’s the tenants, it's getting older," but if I’m being completely honest with myself—and I guess that's why I'm here—I was exactly like this when I was a little kid. Long before I ever picked up a wrench or had to worry about work orders or bosses or paying the mortgage. 

I remember being this exact same way all the way back in grade school. I can still picture my third-grade classroom, and it was just a constant, everyday struggle. My teachers would always pull my parents aside at parent-teacher conferences, and it was always the same exact speech every single year. They always told my mom and dad that I was bright—which honestly almost made it worse, because then everyone just assumed I was being lazy or doing it on purpose! But I really wasn't. I just... my backpack was an absolute black hole. I would do my homework, I swear I would sit at the kitchen table and do it, and then the next morning it was just gone. I misplaced papers constantly. My desk at school looked like a tornado had touched down right on top of it. 

And listening in class was a whole other disaster. When the teacher would stand up front and give out instructions, like, "Okay class, take out your math book, turn to page forty, and do the odd numbers," I would get as far as taking the book out. Then my brain would just drift off, and I'd completely miss the rest of the directions. I'd just be sitting there, maybe looking at a smudge on my desk or staring out the window, and the teacher would always have to come walk down the aisle, tap on my desk, and give me all these extra reminders just to get me to finish my classwork. It was so frustrating. You know, you sit there and all the other kids are just doing the worksheet, and you’re the only one who needs a personal invitation to finish the assignment. So, yeah, it’s definitely not a new thing at all. It’s just that back then it meant a bad note on a report card, and now it means I might lose my chance at a promotion.

symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes their brain drifting off and missing directions when the teacher was speaking to the class.
symptom_reasoning.S004: The patient reports failing to follow through on instructions and needing extra reminders from the teacher to finish classwork.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient describes their backpack as a 'black hole' and their desk as looking like a 'tornado,' indicating severe difficulty with organization.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient states they constantly misplaced papers and frequently lost their completed homework.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient mentions getting easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as a smudge on the desk or staring out the window during class.

turns.doctor_question: Do you often feel physically restless or have a hard time sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
No, not really. I mean, I know some people get all fidgety and just can't stay in their chair to save their lives, but that's never really been my problem at all. If anything, I can sit still for hours. Like, I'll be in my work truck taking my lunch break, you know, just eating a sandwich, and I'll just sort of stare out the windshield at the parking lot. My body is perfectly still the whole time. I don't have that... that urge to get up and pace around or tap my feet or anything. 

My husband actually always teases me that when I sit down on the couch after a long shift to watch the news, I practically turn into a statue because I just zone completely out. So, no, the physical part of it, like staying in one spot, that's completely fine. I don't feel like I have a motor running inside me making me want to jump out of my skin. It's really just that while my body is sitting there perfectly fine and quiet, my mind is completely out to lunch. So yeah, sitting still isn't the issue for me at all, it's just trying to keep my brain in the room while I'm doing it.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient notes that while their body is still, their 'mind is completely out to lunch' and they struggle to 'keep my brain in the room,' indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly denies getting fidgety or having the urge to tap their feet.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient denies having trouble staying in their chair, stating they can sit still for hours.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient answers 'No, not really' to the doctor's question about feeling physically restless.
symptom_reasoning.S014: The patient explicitly denies feeling like they have a 'motor running inside me'.
